title: Living ashtpadi 1
hookLine: Guru Arjan begins with the simplest practice: remember

cards: If you were writing the great bani of peace, where would you start? A philosophy of suffering? A ladder of spiritual stages, beginner to master?
A list of rules? Guru Arjan, the Guru who gathered the scripture, could have begun anywhere. He began with something a child can do, what happens whenever someone you love comes to mind.
No equipment, no training, no special room. He began with remembering.

teach.h: THE BOW, THE WORD, THE DRUM.
teach.b: Look back at the whole first ashtpadi. The salok bows four times. The first stanza says: remember, again and again, and find peace.
The next beats the drum, prabh kai simran: in God's remembrance, fear does not touch, sorrow does not burn. Then the ashtpadi widens the circle.

teach.h: THE ONES WHO REMEMBER ARE RICH.
teach.b: In paraphrase: those who remember God are truly rich, truly honored, truly at rest. Near the end it says something important about where remembering happens.
In paraphrase: the remembrance of God comes in the company of the holy, and it comes to those to whom God gives it. So simran isn't a feat of willpower.
It grows in company, the sangat.

teach.h: A GIFT AS MUCH AS AN EFFORT.
teach.b: In this reading it's a gift as much as an effort, and in the Ardas, Sikhs ask for the gift of the Name rather than claiming it. That's a gentle place to begin. The first ashtpadi doesn't ask you to be holy.
It asks you to remember, among good people, and to ask for the remembering when it won't come. On an ordinary Tuesday, living it might look like a reminder on your phone that says only: remember.
Waheguru, or your own steady word, on the walk from the car.
A friend you sit with who makes remembering easier. Not grand. Just repeated.
In the order Guru Arjan chose, remembering comes first, and the sections ahead build on it.

how: Sikhs carry the first ashtpadi's teaching into the day by repeating Waheguru during ordinary tasks, and by joining the sangat, where Sukhmani says remembrance of God is found.

o: the holy company, where remembering grows
a single quiet hour of prayer, alone
the free meal served in a gurdwara

games.q: the first ashtpadi, start to end — tap the pairs.

s: the first ashtpadi presents remembering as a feat of willpower alone
it says remembrance comes in the company of the holy, and to those God gives it.
Guru Arjan begins Sukhmani with remembering
simro simar simar: the first stanza's first word.
the first ashtpadi calls those who remember God truly rich
truly rich, truly honored, truly at rest.

games.q: you want to keep remembering God through an ordinary week, but it keeps slipping. what does the first ashtpadi point to?
o: the company of the holy, and asking for the gift.
giving up until life is calmer.
games.why: the ashtpadi says remembrance comes in the company of the holy and is given by God.

practice: If your phone is near, set one reminder for later with a one-word label: remember, or Waheguru if you pray.
Then put the phone face down and practice now, so the reminder has somewhere to land: a few slow breaths, the Name or your word on each one.

wordCard.voice: Sangat, the company of the holy: Sukhmani's first section in daily life: bow, remember again and again, and let the remembering grow in good company.

carryVoice: Your line: begin with remembering. It grows best in good company, among good people. That's a week.
